executive_assessment.text: Named marz crop/water risks and Lori–Tavush flood impacts distinguish exposure and vulnerability. PDNA evidence highlights displaced and host households and registration-related recovery barriers for women-headed households.

Older adaptation/crop-insurance plans and the 2026–2030 framework describe intended institutional and peace/resilience capacities; elapsed plan deadlines and future cohesion objectives are not verified results.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2024-11 reports: Flood losses relative to regional GDP are highest in Vayots Dzor, Tavush, Lori and Gegharkunik; the report also locates severe irrigation-water and land-degradation risks in high-poverty marzes.

The 2020 communication's satellite-based assessment for 1984–2017 describes differentiated drought-related crop damage in the Ararat Valley, southwestern Gegharkunik, Kotayk and Gegharkunik. Its damage-frequency categories are not reused as current annual probabilities.
Source dated 2020 reports: By 2070, projected wheat yields fall about 19–20% in Ararat, Kotayk and Gegharkunik, potato yields 21% in Shirak, while wheat yields rise about 8% in Lori.
Source dated 2020 reports: The communication records a crop-insurance pilot launched in 2018: potatoes and cereals against hail and frost in Shirak, and fruit and grapes in Armavir and Ararat.

Source dated 2021-05-13 reports: The 2021–2025 action list scheduled adaptation plans for pilot marzes Shirak and Tavush, then eight more marzes, integrating climate adaptation into regional development planning.

Source dated 2024-10 reports: Lori and Tavush hosted 7% of Nagorno-Karabakh refugees before the May 2024 floods; refugees and host households in Tashir and Alaverdi faced flood-related displacement and damage to homes, food supplies and essential services.

Source dated 2024-10 reports: Field discussions in Lori and Tavush found women-headed households more likely to miss flood compensation when homes or livelihood assets lacked official property registration.

Source dated 2024-10 reports: Flooding damaged eight hydrological stations in the Debed and Aghstev basins, impairing water monitoring; the PDNA calls for modern flood forecasting, risk modeling and early warning, especially in remote areas.

No reviewed primary report establishes that climate change caused conflict or violence in Armenia. The Cooperation Framework states planned resource-competition and social-cohesion pathways, not measured results.
The CCDR's border-conflict context does not identify climate change as a cause of conflict; the May 2024 PDNA records flood impacts but does not attribute the event to anthropogenic climate change.
The NAP's 2021–2025 adaptation measures are plans whose completion was not verified; the Cooperation Framework does not name the border or displacement-affected pilot municipalities.
The Fourth National Communication's crop-yield tables do not identify their emissions pathway; those projections are reported with that limitation.
Conflict-affected farmland rehabilitation and shared restoration/water management are stated response objectives, not demonstrated reduced competition or stronger cohesion.
Named refugee/host flood impacts and registration-related recovery barriers provide differentiated vulnerability evidence without implying that climate caused the displacement conflict.
No complete climate→violence or verified reverse operational insecurity pathway is assembled from these sources.
